options.text: Nothing secret — it is reversible by anyone and uses no key
A one-way hash of the data

questions.explanation: Encoding (Base64) just reformats data for transport; it is keyless and reversible by anyone, providing no confidentiality at all.

questions.prompt: Match each operation to what it provides.
questions.explanation: Encoding is not security, encryption gives confidentiality, hashing gives a one-way fingerprint, and AEAD gives both confidentiality and integrity.

questions.prompt: To send someone a confidential message with public-key crypto, which key do you use?

options.text: The recipient's public key (only their private key can decrypt)

questions.explanation: Encrypt with the recipient's public key; only their matching private key can decrypt. You sign (not encrypt) with your own private key.

questions.prompt: Which are TRUE about hashing? Select all that apply.

options.text: A good hash is one-way — you can't reverse it to the input
MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance
Passwords should be stored with a plain fast hash like SHA-256
A tiny input change produces a very different digest (avalanche)

questions.explanation: Hashes are one-way with an avalanche effect; MD5/SHA-1 are broken for collisions; and passwords need a slow, salted KDF, not a plain fast hash.

questions.prompt: Getting confidentiality AND integrity together in one step uses ____ encryption (e.g. AES-GCM).
questions.explanation: Authenticated encryption (AEAD) modes like AES-GCM provide both confidentiality and integrity, so tampering is detected.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to send a private, authentic message using hybrid crypto.

items.text: Encrypt the message with a fast symmetric key K
Encrypt K with the recipient's public key
Sign the message with your private key
Recipient decrypts K, decrypts the message, and verifies your signature

questions.explanation: Hybrid crypto encrypts data symmetrically, wraps the key with the recipient's public key, signs for authenticity, and the recipient reverses and verifies — the pattern behind TLS.
